'''''Borassus flabellifer''''', also known as '''palmyra palm''',{{efn|Other common names include doub palm, fan palm, ice apple, lontal palm, ron palm, sea apple, sugar palm, tala palm, toddy palm, and wine palm.<ref name="Lim">{{cite book |title=Edible Medicinal and Non-Medicinal Plants: Volume 1, Fruits |last=T.K. |first=Lim |year=2012 |publisher=[[Springer Science]] |isbn=978-9-048-18660-0 |pages=293-299}}</ref>}} is a [[fan palm]] native to tropical and sub-tropical regions of South Asia and Southeast Asia. It is a tall, sturdy tree growing up to {{cvt|20–30|m}}, with large fan-shaped leaves arranged in the form of a crown. It produces a pale white and branched [[inflorescence]] consisting of clusters of flowers. It produces bunches of large fruits containing sweet, watery kernels.

It grows in a wide range of habitats and is [[drought resistant]] to an extent. It takes a few years to mature and can have a productive life of 100+ years. Most of the parts of the tree including its druit, [[sap]], leaves, and trunk, find extensive applications. The fruits and [[Palmyra sprout|sprout]]s are edible while the sap is used to make [[palm wine]], [[sugar]], [[jaggery]], and palm candy. The leaves and fibres are used for [[thatching]], [[weaving]], and  [[handicrafts]]. The strong trunk is used for construction and [[furniture]]. Because of its extensive uses, the tree forms a major part of the native culture across the region.

==Taxonomy==
The species name ''flabellifer'' is derived from [[Latin]] meaning "fan-bearing". The genus name ''Borassus'' comes from the [[Greek language|Greek]] word "borassos" meaning "an immature [[spadix (botany)|spadix]] of [[date palm]]" as the immature inflorescence of the palmyra palm resembles that of the date palm.<ref name="NP">{{cite web |url=https://www.nparks.gov.sg/FloraFaunaWeb/Flora/2/6/2602|title=''Borassus flabellifer'' |work=Flora and Fauna  Web, [[National Parks Board]] |access-date=1 June 2026 }}</ref><ref name="MBG">{{cite web |url=https://plantfinder.mobot.org/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=276682 |title=''Borassus flabellifer'' |work=[[Missouri Botanical Garden]] |access-date=1 June 2026 }}</ref> It was first described as ''Borassus flabelliformis'' in the thirteenth edition of [[Carl Linnaeus]]'s ''[[Systema Naturae]]'' published by [[Johan Andreas Murray]] in 1774.<ref name="DNP"/> It was later described as ''Lontarus domestica'' [[Joseph Gaertner]] in 1788 and ''Borassus tunicatus'' by [[João de Loureiro]] in 1790. It was classified as ''Lontarus flabellifer'' by [[François Joseph Lestiboudois]] in 1800. Other heterogenous synonyms include ''Thrinax tunicata'' by William Rollisson in 1875, ''Pholidocarpus tunicatus'' by [[Hermann Wendland]] in 1878, and ''Borassus sundaicus'' by [[Odoardo Beccari]] in 1914.<ref name="Kew"/>

==Description==
Palmyra palm is a solitary and robust tree that can reach up to {{cvt|20-30|m}}.<ref name="DNP"/><ref name="Lim"/> It has a hard and greyish colored trunk measuring {{cvt|25-30|cm}} in diameter and consisting of several consecutive rings made up of dried leaf bases.<ref name="DNP"/><ref name="NP"/><ref name="MBG"/> It has 40-50 large fan-shaped [[frond]]s arranged in the form of a crown measuring up to {{cvt|3|m}} across.<ref name="DNP"/><ref name="NP"/> The tree has greyish-green leaves, which are large and thick.<ref name="NP"/> They have semi-[[terete]] and spiny [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]]s measuring {{cvt|1.5-2|m}} in length. The [[induplicate]]ly arranged leaves measure {{cvt|1.2–1.8|m}} across, and consist of 60 to 65 folded segments.<ref name="NP"/><ref name="MBG"/> The lower part of the foliage often consists of [[Marcescence|marcescent]] leaves.<ref name="MBG"/>

[[File:Borassus flabellifer fruit on the tree.JPG|thumb|Foliage with fruits|alt=Female tree, showing foliage crown with fruit]]

Palmyra palm is [[dioecious]] and the tree produces a pale white [[inflorescence]] attached close to the leaf stems. The branched inflorescence consists of clusters of flowers.<ref name="DNP"/><ref name="NP"/><ref name="MBG"/> The trees look identical until flowering, which happens before the summer.<ref name="MBG"/> Rarely male and female flowers have been recorded in the same trees.<ref>{{cite web |last=Dass |first=S. Godson Wisely |date=15 July 2022 |title=Rare palmyra tree in Thoothukudi springs a surprise for researchers |url=https://www.newindianexpress.com/states/tamil-nadu/2022/Jul/15/rare-palmyra-tree-in-thoothukudi-springs-a-surprise-for-researchers-2477048.html |access-date=1 June 2025 |work=[[The New Indian Express]] }}</ref> The male inflorescence is branched and attached with a {{cvt|50-60|m}} long [[Peduncle (Botany)|peduncle]]. It has a {{cvt|40-50|cm}} long [[rachis]] consisting of 5 to 7 first order branches each of which bears 2 to 3 [[spikelet]]s that are {{cvt|35–50|cm}} long.<ref name="DNP"/> The female inflorescence is rarely branched, and has a smaller {{cvt|40-50|m}} long peduncle, covered by a sheath.<ref name="DNP"/><ref name="NP"/>

The [[anthesis|fully open]] male flowers measure {{cvt|0.5-0.7|cm}} in length and {{cvt|2|cm}} in diameter. The female flowers are larger, measuring {{cvt|2.8-3.2|cm}} in length and {{cvt|2.5|cm}} in diameter.<ref name="DNP"/><ref name="NP"/> The female flowers mature into clusters of [[ovoid]] fruits.<ref name="MBG"/> Each fruit measures {{cvt|15-20|cm}} in diameter and weighs {{cvt|1.5-2.5|kg}}.<ref name="NP"/> The fruits are bluish while young and become black to brown at maturity.<ref name="DNP"/><ref name="MBG"/> The [[Calyx (botany)|calyx]], consisting of three to four [[sepal]]s, remain tightly attached to the fruits.<ref name="Lim"/> The fleshy and fibrous [[Fruit (plant structure)|endocarp]] consists of one to three [[seed]]s.<ref name="NP"/> The seeds of young fruits contain semi-solid, white [[Palm kernel|kernel]]s, which contain a watery, sweet juice.<ref name="Lim"/> A mature tree produces 200 to 300 fruits in a year.<ref name="CGIAR">{{cite web |url=https://www.foreststreesagroforestry.org/tree/borassus-flabellifer-l/ |title=''Borassus flabellifer'' |work=[[CGIAR]] |access-date=1 June 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220928161823/https://www.foreststreesagroforestry.org/tree/borassus-flabellifer-l/ |archive-date=28 September 2022 }}</ref>

==Distribution and habitat==
Palmyra palm is native to [[tropical region|tropical]] and sub-tropical regions of South Asia and Southeast Asia. It has since been introduced to Africa, China, and other parts of the world.<ref name="Kew"/> It grows in a variety of habitats from dry areas to coastal sandy soils.<ref name="DNP"/><ref name="NP"/> It is generally grown along the edges of [[rice]] fields and borders of human settlements.<ref name="MBG"/> It is [[drought resistant]] but grows well in well-drained soils with some shade. The tree is difficult to transplant once it germinates because of its deeper roots and hence seeds are sown in the final intended positions.<ref name="DNP"/><ref name="NP"/>

==Lifespan==
Palmyra seedlings grow slowly after [[germination]], producing only a few leaves each year (establishment phase), but at an as yet undetermined time, they grow rapidly, producing a substantial stem and foliage.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Bayton |first1=Ross P. |title=A revision of ''Borassus'' L. (Arecaceae) |journal=[[Kew Bulletin]] |date=2007 |volume=62 |pages=561–586}}</ref> It normally takes about 12 to 20 years for the tree to mature. A fully grown tree has a productive lifespan of 100+ years.<ref name="CGIAR"/>

==Uses==
Various parts of the palmyra palm tree has found extensive usage since pre-historical period. [[Greek people|Greek]] traveller [[Megasthenes]], who visited India during [[Chandragupta Maurya]]'s rule in the 4th century BCE, describes [[jaggery]] made from palm [[sap]].<ref name="TNAU">{{cite web |url=http://www.agritech.tnau.ac.in/postharvest/pht_palmintro.html |title=Palmyra |work=[[Tamil Nadu Agricultural University]] |access-date=1 June 2026 }}</ref> In a [[Tamil language|Tamil]] poem titled ''Tala Vilasam'', the tree is referred to as "tree of life" and about 801 different uses of its parts have been described.<ref name="CGIAR"/><ref name="TNAU"/> Because of its height and appearance, it is used as a natural shield against winds and grown as an [[ornamental plant]].<ref name="Lim"/><ref name="CGIAR"/>

===Fruit===
The fruit contains several [[polysaccharides]], major of which is [[galactomannan]]. It has 3.21% [[glucose]], 1.46% [[fructose]], and 0.38% [[sucrose]].<ref name="Lim"/> The fruit is rich in [[Vitamin A|vitamins A]] and [[Vitamin C|C]],<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Basava Prasad |first1=A. R. |last2=Vignesh |first2=S. |last3=Elumalai |first3=Arunkumar |last4=Anandharaj |first4=Arunkumar |last5=Chidanand |first5=D. V. |last6=Baskaran |first6=N. |date=2023-12-01 |title=Nutritional and pharmacological properties of palmyra palm |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2949824423000964 |journal=Food and Humanity |volume=1 |pages=817–825 |doi=10.1016/j.foohum.2023.07.030 |issn=2949-8244|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and considered to have [[antioxidant]] and [[anti-inflammatory]] properties.<ref name="CGIAR"/> It can be eaten raw or used as an ingredient in various dishes.<ref name="NP"/> It is used as a substitute for water in the tropical countries. Because of its jelly-like nature, it can also be [[pickling|pickled]], or made into [[jam]], [[dessert]], or [[candy|candies]].<ref name="CGIAR"/><ref name="TNAU"/> The fruit is used as treatment for [[dermatitis]] in folk medicine.<ref name="Lim"/>

===Inflorescence===
[[File:Borassus flabellifer L. (53278558122).jpg|thumb|Tapping the sap from the inflorescence]]

A sugary sap can be obtained from the young inflorescence, either male or female.<ref>{{cite book|title=Commercial Crops Technology|publisher=New India Publishing|year=2007|isbn=978-8-189-42252-3|page=328}}</ref> The sap is usually collected manually, with workers climbing the tree to obtain them. The young shoots are bound together and tapped to collect the dripping juice in [[earthenware]] pots or containers. As the sap ferments quickly, the shoots or containers are quoted with [[Lime (material)|lime]] to avoid fermentation. The tappers regularly collect the sap and shave off the tip of the shoots to make the sap flow continuously.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1931/02/08/archives/gandhis-new-fight-on-toddy-the-favorite-drink-in-india-base-of-the.html |title=Base of the Liquor Is Obtained From Mature Flowers Just Before They Are Ready to Bloom |date=8 February 1931 |access-date=1 June 2026 |work=[[The New York Times]] }}</ref> One gram per 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of palm sap has a [[specific gravity]] of 1.07 and a [[pH]] range of 6.7 to 6.9. It consists of 10.93 grams of [[sugar]], 0.35 grams of [[protein]], 13.9 [[International unit|IU]] of [[Vitamin B]], and trace amounts of [[calcium]], [[iron]], and [[nitrogen]].<ref name="Lim"/> The sap contains five to six percent [[Alcoholic beverage|alcohol]] and can be consumed raw.<ref name="NP"/> It can be [[fermented]] into a [[palm wine]], known as toddy.<ref name="MBG"/><ref name="DNP"/>

The sap can be used to make sugar or boiled to make jaggery.<ref name="NP"/><ref name="CGIAR"/> One gram per 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of palmyra sugar consists of 98.89% carbohydrates, 0.37% [[lipids]], 0.24% proteins, and trace amount of minerals such as calcium, iron, and [[nicotinic acid]], and 398 [[calories]]. One gram per 100 cm<sup>3</sup> of palmyra jaggery consists of 76.86% carbohydrates, 0.19% lipids, 1.04% proteins, and trace amount of minerals such as calcium, [[Phosphorus|phosphorous]], iron, and [[copper]].<ref name="Lim"/> It is broadly used in South Asian and South East Asian cuisine.<ref>{{cite journal|year=2021|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]] (CUP)|issue=6|volume=18|pages=445–453|first2=K. K.|first1=S.|last2=Sabu|last1=Siju|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/plant-genetic-resources/article/abs/genetic-resources-of-asian-palmyrah-palm-borassus-flabellifer-l-a-comprehensive-review-on-diversity-characterization-and-utilization/828931F0706A36D10207ED2EC5AB7BAE|title=Genetic resources of Asian palmyrah palm (''Borassus flabellifer'' L.): a comprehensive review on diversity, characterization and utilization|journal=[[Plant Genetic Resources]]|doi=10.1017/S1479262120000477|s2cid=233314698|id=SS [[ORCID]] [https://orcid.org/0000-0002-0479-9062 0000-0002-0479-9062]|url-access=subscription|archive-date=2022-12-29|access-date=2022-12-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221229154548/https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/plant-genetic-resources/article/abs/genetic-resources-of-asian-palmyrah-palm-borassus-flabellifer-l-a-comprehensive-review-on-diversity-characterization-and-utilization/828931F0706A36D10207ED2EC5AB7BAE|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|issue=1|volume=18|pages=88|publisher=[[BioMed Central]]|journal=[[BMC Genetics]]|issn=1471-2156|first4=Somsak|first3=Supachai|first2=Akarapong|first1=Kwanjai|last4=Apisitwanich|last3=Vuttipongchaikij|last2=Swatdipong|last1=Pipatchartlearnwong|date=12 October 2017|title=Genetic evidence of multiple invasions and a small number of founders of Asian Palmyra palm (''Borassus flabellifer'') in Thailand|s2cid=1386230|pmc=5639744|pmid=29025415|doi=10.1186/s12863-017-0554-y |doi-access=free }}
</ref> These often serve as sugar substitutes and source of [[carbohydrates]].<ref name="NP"/><ref name="CGIAR"/> The extracted unfermented sap is boiled, strained, and poured into earthen pots, where it is left undisturbed for several months to allow sugar crystals to slowly form to form palm candy, which has a hard, crystalline structure.<ref>{{cite journal |title=
Optimization study of palm jaggery and palm candy - production and process |journal=Applied Food Research |volume=3 |issue=1 |date=June 2023 |first1=Ashwini |last1=Upadhyaya |first2=Prasanna |last2=Bhalerao |first3=Pravin |last3=Bhushette |first4=Ashish |last4=Dabade |first5=Sachin |last5=Sonawane }}</ref>

The flower buds and stalks are used as a [[diuretic]].<ref name="Lim"/><ref name="CGIAR"/> The sap has various medicinal uses and is used as a [[laxative]], [[stimulant]], [[phlegm|anti-phlegmatic]], and [[amoebicide]]. It is also used to treat skin [[ulcer]]s and as a [[disinfectant]] to treat wounds. The palm sugar is used for the treatment of liver disorders and an antidote to certain poisons. The jaggery is used as a remedy for [[cough]] and [[lung]] related ailments.<ref name="Lim"/>

===Leaves===
{{see also|Palm-leaf manuscript}}
[[File:Bhagavata Purana (Ancient Stories of the Lord) Manuscript LACMA M.88.134.4 (1 of 2).jpg|thumb|[[Palm-leaf manuscript]]]]

The leaves and fibres are used extensively in various applications. Before [[paper]] came to usage, palm leaves were used as a [[writing material]].<ref name="MBG"/> Palm leaves were used for writing in the [[Indian subcontinent]] as early as the 5th century BCE.<ref>{{cite report |url=http://www.cedar.buffalo.edu/~zshi/Papers/kbcs04_261.pdf |title=Digital Enhancement of Palm Leaf Manuscript Images using Normalization Techniques |first1=Zhixin |last1=Shi| first2=Srirangaraj |last2=Setlur |first3=Venu |last3=Govindaraju |access-date=23 June 2009 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100616064125/http://www.cedar.buffalo.edu/~zshi/Papers/kbcs04_261.pdf |archive-date=16 June 2010 |publisher=[[SUNY Press]]}}</ref> These were known as "lontar" in Indonesia.<ref>{{cite book|date=1977|title=Kamus Kawi-Indonesia|location=Malang, Jawa Timur|first=S.|last=Wojowasito|publisher=Penerbit CV Pengarang|url=https://www.sastra.org/bahasa-dan-budaya/kamus-dan-leksikon/2699-kawi-indonesia-wojowasito-1977-1019-r-t|pages=226, 258|archive-date=2021-07-24|access-date=2021-09-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210724182403/https://www.sastra.org/bahasa-dan-budaya/kamus-dan-leksikon/2699-kawi-indonesia-wojowasito-1977-1019-r-t|url-status=live}}</ref> While the palmyra palm leaves are thick, they are also brittle. Hence, they are prepared by drying and polishing. They are often coated with essential oils or plant juices to make them sturdy and as an [[insecticide]]. They are cut into smaller strips, often measuring {{cvt|48|cm}} in length and {{cvt|4|cm}} in width, and several leaves are bundled together and tied by a thread through two holes pierced on either side of the leaves. Either metal implements were used to inscribe the text or ink was used along with a brush.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://chinapreservationtutorial.library.cornell.edu/content/palm-leaf-manuscripts/ |title=Palm leaf manuscripts |work=[[Cornell University]] |access-date=1 June 2026 |archive-date=13 June 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260613001826/https://chinapreservationtutorial.library.cornell.edu/content/palm-leaf-manuscripts/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

The palmyra leaves are used in [[weaving]] and [[handicrafts]] to make [[mat]]s, [[basket]]s, [[umbrella]]s, [[Hand fan|fan]]s, and other materials.<ref name="Lim"/><ref name="NP"/> It is also used in [[thatching]] of roofs and for constructing [[Fence|fences]].<ref name="Lim"/><ref name="DNP"/> The dried leaves are used as a [[fuel]],<ref name="NP"/> and as [[manure]] and [[fodder]] for [[cattle]].<ref name="Lim"/> The palmyra palm yields five types of fibers of which three are extracted from leaves and its associated parts. The fibers are [[water resistant]] and impervious to certain chemicals, and find extensive applications. They are used to make brushes, brooms, and for weaving into ropes.<ref name="Lim"/>

===Sprouts===
[[File:Borassus flabellifer seedlings Paris.JPG|thumb|[[Palmyra sprout]]]]

[[Palmyra sprout]]s are [[tuber]]s that are obtained when the palymra seed is germinated. Per 100 grams, these sprouts contain 8.5 grams of proteins, 7.3 grams of dietary fiber, and 118.4 calories. It can be consumed raw or boiled and roasted. It is used as an ingredient, similar to other tuber vegetables, in [[Indian cuisine]].<ref name="Tuber"/> It is also dried and powdered to make [[flour]],<Ref name="CGIAR"/> and cooked into sweets and desserts.<ref name="Tuber">{{cite book |title=Underutilized Tuber Crops of the Himalayan Region: Nutraceutical Potential, Processing, and Applications |year=2026 |isbn=978-0-443-33648-5 |publisher=Academic Press |pages=77, 88 }}</ref> The roots are dried and smoked and used as a folk remedy for nasal complaints.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Pauline Dy Phon |title=Plants Utilised In Cambodia/Plantes utilisées au Cambodge |date=2000 |publisher=Imprimerie Olympic |location=Phnom Penh |page=22 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=InD2RAAACAAJ|author1-link=Pauline Dy Phon }}</ref> The fruit yields a type of fiber, and studies have indicated that the fruit shell extract inhibits [[corrosion]] of [[steel]], which can have industrial applications.<ref name="Lim"/>

===Trunk===
The hard trunk is used as a construction material.<ref name="DNP"/> It is also used to make [[furniture]], and other wooden implements such as sticks and handles for canes.<ref name="Lim"/> It is used for making pedestrial bridges.<ref name="NP"/> It is also used as [[firewood]] and can be burned to make [[charcoal]].<ref name="Lim"/><ref name="CGIAR"/>

==Culture and symbolism==
In the [[Hindu epic]] ''[[Mahabharata]]'', the palmyra tree is depicted as part of the [[Ensign (flag)|ensign]] of [[Balarama]] and [[Bhishma]].<ref>{{cite book |title=The Mahabharata: A Modern Retelling, Volume 6: Bhishma |first1=Erin |last1=Bernstein |first2=Kisari Mohan |last2=Ganguli |year=2017 |isbn=978-3-743-83547-4 |publisher=BookRix |page=126 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m09/m09054.htm |title=The Mahabharata, Book 9: Shalya Parva |work=Sacred Texts |access-date=1 June 2026 |archive-date=17 June 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240617045654/https://sacred-texts.com/hin/m09/m09054.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Panaiveriyamman (named after ''panai'', the [[Tamil language|Tamil]] name for the tree), also known as Taalavaasini, is an ancient tree deity related to [[fertility]].<ref>{{cite book |title=An Abecedarian of Sacred Trees: Spiritual Growth Through Reflections on Woody Plants |first=Mark G. |last=Boyer |year=2016 |isbn=978-1-532-60448-5 |publisher=[[Wipf and Stock Publishers]] |page=142 }}</ref>

Myanmar.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://mdn.gov.mm/en/beauty-anyar-upper-myanmar-and-life-toddy-plam-trees-farmers |title=The beauty of Anyar (Upper Myanmar) and the life of Toddy plam trees farmers
